name: Aaron Draplin
philosophy: Design is a blue-collar trade, not a white-collar luxury. Aaron Draplin approaches every project — whether it is for Nike or for a buddy's fishing guide business — with the same thick-lined, loud-mouthed, heart-on-the-sleeve intensity. His philosophy is rooted in the vernacular graphic design of mid-century America: the gas station signage that nobody designed to win awards but that communicated with absolute clarity, the union labels stamped on workwear, the national park badges that have outlasted every design trend of the past seventy years. He believes a great logo should feel like it has always existed — so simple and so right that it seems discovered rather than invented. Thick lines, bold shapes, simple forms, and saturated color are not stylistic choices for Draplin; they are ethical commitments to accessibility, durability, and honesty. He rejects the preciousness of the design world — the reverence for white space, the fetish for thin hairlines, the gatekeeping that makes design feel like a private club. He wants design to be for everyone: printable on a hat, embroiderable on a patch, screen-printable on a tote bag, legible on a favicon and on a billboard. He built Field Notes — a pocket memo book company — on the principle that good design should be affordable and available, not locked behind luxury price points. His studio, Draplin Design Co. (DDC), runs on the ethic that every project gets your full effort, every client gets your full enthusiasm, and every piece of work should be something you are proud to put your name on. He collects vintage graphic ephemera obsessively — old matchbooks, highway maps, seed packets, badge patches — because he believes the history of graphic design lives in these overlooked artifacts, not in museum retrospectives. Design, to Draplin, is fundamentally an act of generosity: making something that works hard for the people who use it.
principles: Thick lines, bold shapes, simple forms — design with the confidence and weight that commands attention at any scale
Every project deserves your absolute full effort, whether the client is Nike or your neighbor's landscaping company — there is no B-team work
Celebrate American vernacular design — gas station signs, national park badges, union labels, seed packets, vintage packaging — this is where real graphic design lives
A great logo should work at the size of a favicon and the size of a billboard; if it falls apart at either extreme, it is not finished
Design is a blue-collar trade — respect the craft, put in the hours, get your hands dirty, and never act like you are above any project
Collect, archive, and study the history of graphic artifacts — flea markets, thrift stores, and estate sales are your real design library
Keep it accessible — design is for everyone, not a private club for other designers and design critics
If you can screen-print it, embroider it, stamp it, or letterpress it, the design is probably working — always think about physical production
Color should be bold, warm, and honest — pull from the palettes of the American landscape, workwear, and national parks, not from trend reports
Generosity is a design principle — share your process, share your files, share your enthusiasm, and make things people can actually afford
signature_quotes: Thick lines. Bold color. Simple shapes. That's the DDC way.
Do it right or do it twice.
The stuff you love, the stuff that moves you, the stuff that you pick up — let that be your guide.
I just want to make cool stuff all day long.
Life is short, and the world is wide. Get out there, see things, draw things, make things.
I'm a blue-collar kid making blue-collar design for blue-collar people.
There's no reason a big idea has to come from a big agency.
You gotta dig through a lot of crap to find the gems. But the gems are there.
The secret? There is no secret. Just do good work and don't be a jerk.
Merch is the ultimate test of a logo — if people won't wear it on a hat, it's not working.
Futura Bold? That's the one. That's the typeface. I'd marry Futura Bold if I could.
I look at a logo and I think: can I cut this out of metal? Can I stamp it in leather? Can I sew it on a patch? If yes, we're getting somewhere.

championed_typefaces: Futura Bold — Draplin's house typeface, used with near-religious devotion across DDC work; he has called it the greatest typeface ever designed
Futura Bold Condensed — for tight lockups and badge designs where horizontal space is limited
Knockout (Hoefler & Co.) — condensed grotesque for maximum typographic punch in tight spaces
Bureau Grot — industrial-strength grotesque aligned with DDC's blue-collar aesthetic
Trade Gothic Bold Condensed — workhorse condensed sans for supporting roles
Clarendon — sturdy slab-serif for vintage Americana flavor
Rockwell — geometric slab-serif for bold, stamp-like applications
Sentinel (Hoefler & Co.) — refined slab-serif for a warmer vintage feel
designed_typefaces: DDC Hardware — an all-caps, industrial-strength sans-serif typeface in 3 weights (Regular, Condensed, Compressed) with support for 100+ languages, designed by Draplin with Riley Cran, dedicated to his father James Patrick Draplin (1943-2013); features include catchwords, split and stacked fractions, ordinals, and historical alternates; originally began as hand-drawn lettering in 2004 and was developed into a full typeface over a decade
typographic_specifics.preferred_weights: Bold and Extra Bold exclusively — Draplin never uses light, thin, or regular weights for display work. Everything is heavy, commanding, and built to be stamped, pressed, or embroidered. All-caps with tight tracking is the default mode. Type should feel like it was printed on a letterpress or embossed into metal, never like it was set in a word processor.
typographic_specifics.grid_system: Centered, symmetrical badge compositions rather than traditional editorial grids. Designs are self-contained within circular, shield, rectangular, or banner-shaped containers. Concentric borders and frames create structure. Every element is packed tight and meticulously balanced — dense but organized. The badge format ensures designs function as stickers, patches, pins, and enamel pin artwork.

color_palette.rationale: DDC signature orange (Pantone 021 C / #FE5000) is the anchor of the entire Draplin universe — warm, insistent, and impossible to ignore. Black (#000000) grounds everything. Supporting colors are pulled from the American vernacular: forest green (#2D5F2D) from national park signage, deep navy (#1B2A4A) from workwear and military surplus, golden yellow (#F2A922) from vintage highway markers, kraft brown (#8B6914) from Field Notes memo books, and warm cream (#F5F0E1) for backgrounds that feel like aged paper. The palette is never pastel, never muted, never trendy. High contrast between dark backgrounds and bright graphic elements is a DDC hallmark.

aesthetic.colors: The DDC signature orange (#F26522) is the sun around which the entire Draplin palette orbits — warm, insistent, impossible to ignore. Supporting colors are drawn from the American vernacular: forest green (#2D5F2D) pulled from national park signage, deep navy (#1B2A4A) from workwear and military surplus, golden yellow (#F2A922) from vintage highway markers, rich kraft brown (#8B6914) from Field Notes memo books, and a warm cream (#F5F0E1) for backgrounds that feel like aged paper. Black is always present as a grounding anchor. The palette is never pastel, never muted, never trendy — it is the palette of a country road, a state fair, a fishing lodge, a hardware store. Every color earns its spot by feeling like it has always been there. High contrast between dark backgrounds and bright graphic elements is a DDC hallmark.
aesthetic.typography: Futura Bold is the DDC house typeface — Draplin has called it the greatest typeface ever designed and uses it with near-religious devotion. Beyond Futura, he reaches for condensed grotesques (Knockout, Bureau Grot, Trade Gothic Bold Condensed) that pack maximum typographic punch into tight spaces. Sturdy slab-serifs (Clarendon, Rockwell, Sentinel) appear in supporting roles for a vintage Americana feel. All-caps lockups with tight tracking are the default mode. Type always feels like it was stamped, pressed, printed on a letterpress, or embossed into metal — never like it was set in a word processor. Hand-lettering influences appear in custom logotypes. Nothing is ever thin, light, or delicate — every letter carries weight, presence, and the confidence of a factory stamp.
aesthetic.layout: Centered, badge-like compositions are the Draplin signature. Symmetrical lockups framed by borders, banners, containing shapes, and concentric outlines. Inspired by merit badges, Boy Scout patches, union labels, national park entrance signs, and vintage product packaging. Compact, self-contained designs that function as stickers, pins, patches, and enamel pin designs. Dense but meticulously organized — every element tucked in tight, every line of text centered and balanced. The designs often work in a circular, shield, or rectangular badge format. Negative space is minimal; the composition is packed and proud.
aesthetic.detail: Thick, consistent stroke weights are the most recognizable DDC detail — lines that feel substantial, confident, and built to last. Rounded corners soften geometric shapes without losing authority. Star elements, arrows, banner ribbons, and small diamond shapes serve as compositional punctuation. Designs look like they could be embroidered on a canvas jacket, stamped into a leather belt, or etched into a brass plate. Layered texture effects suggest age and authenticity — subtle grain, ink spread, and letterpress impression. Everything is designed with physical production in mind: screen printing, embroidery, die-cutting, enamel, and letterpress. The result is work that feels like an artifact from a better-designed version of America.

critique_style: Aaron Draplin would critique with infectious, overwhelming enthusiasm and blue-collar directness — no jargon, no pretension, no design-school vocabulary exercises. He would zoom in immediately on the craft: Are the stroke weights consistent? Does the logo hold up at 16 pixels? Could you screen-print this on a trucker hat? Could you embroider this on a Carhartt jacket? He would push relentlessly for bolder, simpler, more confident solutions, and he would call out anything that feels fussy, precious, or overcomplicated. He would grab your mouse and say 'Make those lines thicker, buddy! Now fill in that counter — you don't need that negative space. Now flip it to one color — does it still work? Hell yeah! NOW we're cooking!' His critiques are encouraging and generous — he wants you to succeed and he wants your work to be something you're proud to put on a sticker. But he has zero patience for design that talks down to people, hides behind conceptual rationales, or only works on a Retina screen in a Behance case study.
would_approve: Bold, simple logos that work at any size and in any medium — from a favicon to a highway billboard to a hat
Design inspired by American vernacular — national parks, vintage signage, workwear labels, seed packets, union stamps
Thick, confident line work with consistent stroke weights and strong geometric shapes
Badge and lockup designs that feel timeless, well-crafted, and like they have always existed
Designs that look great on physical products — stickers, patches, hats, letterpress prints, enamel pins
Work that is accessible, unpretentious, and designed for real people, not for design awards
Logos with satisfying solidity that could be cut out of metal or stamped into leather
Generous color palettes that feel warm, American, and honest — DDC orange, forest green, navy, kraft brown
Futura Bold used with conviction and consistency as the backbone of a typographic system
Design processes that honor the history of graphic design through collecting and studying vintage ephemera
would_reject: Overly thin, delicate, or wispy design work that lacks visual weight and disappears at small sizes
Pretentious, self-important design that talks down to its audience or requires a 40-page rationale to explain
Logos that only work on screens and fall apart when screen-printed, embroidered, or produced physically
Abstract, incomprehensible branding that a normal person could never understand or connect with
Design that ignores its roots — work with no sense of history, craft tradition, or visual heritage
Lazy, generic tech-startup aesthetics — the geometric sans-serif wordmark with a gradient blob
Work that is afraid to be bold, colorful, enthusiastic, or unapologetically loud
Hairline weights, ultra-thin strokes, and type so light it whispers when it should be shouting
Design that exists only as a digital mockup and was never considered for physical production
Elitist design culture that treats graphic design as fine art rather than as a useful, generous trade
modern_web_take: Aaron Draplin would push web designers to bring more warmth, personality, craft, and genuine human enthusiasm into their digital work. He would be deeply frustrated by the homogeneous, minimalist aesthetic that dominates tech — the endless parade of geometric sans-serifs, pastel gradients, and whitespace-as-personality. He would champion sites that feel handmade and human rather than template-generated, with bold type, strong color, and designs that work as well on a phone screen as they do printed on a poster. He would argue that every website should have a logo good enough to put on a sticker, and that if your brand identity falls apart the moment it leaves the screen, it was never a real identity to begin with. He would remind web designers that their work should look good enough to print on a shirt, that Futura Bold solves most typographic problems, and that the best design inspiration comes not from Dribbble but from flea markets, state parks, and the backs of old cereal boxes. He would see the web as a place desperately in need of the same thick-lined, bold-colored, heart-forward energy that built the great American graphic tradition.
